passage: The goat wasn't hurt, only startled, but the Thursday haat in Barpeta Road didn't wait to find out. Within a minute Bhupen, still astride his cycle, was ringed by people. "Blind or what?" "These boys ride like kings!" "Whose son is he?" Voices came from behind, from above the vegetable baskets, from a man he had never seen. Bhupen tried to say sorry, but every time he turned to one face, three others were shouting. His throat closed. His cycle bell rang by itself as someone shoved the handlebar. Then Alka, his cousin, pushed through with the goat's owner beside her, the old tea-seller who knew them both. "Bhupen-da, just talk to Kaka," she said. One man, one face. Bhupen finally found his words.

qa.a: Alka, Bhupen's cousin, pushed through with the goat's owner, the old tea-seller who knew them both.

qa.a: Alka brought one person who mattered, the goat's owner, so Bhupen could talk to one face instead of a crowd and finally found his words.

passage: Zanele missed the last penalty on Saturday. By Sunday night the school sports page had three hundred comments under the match photo, most from accounts with cartoon pictures and no real names. Some said she had thrown the game. Some just posted her face with a crying filter. She kept refreshing, hoping one would be reasonable enough to answer, but there was no one to answer; each reply was a new stranger. On Monday in Durban, Omar found her in the changing room staring at her boots. "It's not the whole school," he said. "It's a crowd with no faces." He walked with her to Coach Dlamini, who read the whole thread, sat down beside her, and said, "You missed a kick. You did nothing wrong. I'm asking the school to take this down today."

qa.a: She felt desperate and overwhelmed, hoping one comment would be reasonable enough to answer, but every reply came from a new stranger.

qa.q: Which step made the difference for Zanele on Monday?

passage: The house football final ended with Vishal's own goal. By the time he reached the corridor, it was full: thirty, maybe forty students from Tagore House, all shouting at once. "Traitor!" "Who even picked him?" Someone kicked his bag along the floor. Vishal, fourteen, turned to answer one boy, and three others shouted over him from behind. Every face was a different face. Mr Dsouza came at once, cleared the corridor in a minute and sat with Vishal on the stairs. "It was one bad bounce, and none of this is your fault," he said. He walked Vishal to the counsellor's room himself and phoned his mother before the last bell.

passage:
To: Mr Hemant Rao, school counsellor
Subject: I don't know what to do

Sir,

Since yesterday someone made an account using my photo and posted that I cheated in the science exam. Now there are more than two hundred comments. Most are from accounts with no real names. People I don't know are messaging me. Every time I delete one, five more come. I tried replying to one to explain, but I can't explain to two hundred people. I haven't slept. I didn't go to school today.

Raghav, Class 10B

Reply, 4:40 pm same day:

Raghav, thank you for telling me, beta. None of this is your fault. Please don't reply to any of them. Take screenshots and keep them. I have just spoken to your mother on the phone; she is on her way home to be with you. I have reported the account to the principal, and we will meet with both of you first thing tomorrow.

Mr Rao

qa.q: How many comments were there on the post about Raghav?
qa.a: There were more than two hundred comments.

qa.q: Why did Raghav feel he could not explain himself?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed because the comments came from hundreds of nameless accounts, so there was no single person to explain to.

qa.q: Which steps in Mr Rao's reply help Raghav most?
qa.a: He tells Raghav it is not his fault, says not to reply, asks for screenshots, calls his mother that day and reports the account to the principal.

qa.q: How might Raghav's mother feel after the counsellor's phone call?
qa.a: She would likely be worried and upset for her son, but relieved that the school acted quickly and that she can be home with him.

grounding: A student mobbed by hundreds of anonymous comments feels overwhelmed with no one to reason with, and a counsellor responds the same day.

passage: Irfan, you asked what it was like. Okay. I'm Rekha, class ten. After I reported cheating in the pre-boards, someone put my number in a big class group. By evening there were over a hundred messages. People I'd never spoken to. "Snitch." "Watch your back." Voice notes, stickers, my photo with a clown face. I kept trying to reply to one person, explain, and ten more messages came. There was no one to argue with. It was like shouting at a wave. I sat on the bathroom floor shaking. Then my Amma knocked. I showed her the phone. She sat with me, took screenshots, left the group for me, and called my class teacher that same night. The teacher called the principal before we'd even had dinner. It still hurts. But that night I wasn't alone with the wave.

qa.q: How many messages were there by evening?
qa.a: By evening there were over a hundred messages.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling on the bathroom floor?
qa.a: Rekha felt overwhelmed and frightened, shaking because there was no single person to reason with.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Amma stayed with Rekha, saved screenshots, left the group and called the class teacher that same night, so an adult could stop the attack.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when she saw the phone?
qa.a: Amma was likely shocked and protective, which is why she acted at once instead of waiting.

grounding: A student mobbed by over a hundred hostile messages feels overwhelmed with no single person to reason with, and an adult responds the same night.

passage: Leela, you asked why I don't like big crowds. Let me tell you about the cricket match in 1998. I'm Raghav dada, and I was fifteen, fielding for our school in the district final. I dropped the catch that lost us the cup. When I walked off, the whole stand of our own supporters turned on me. Hundreds of people. Whistles, boos, someone threw a bottle. I couldn't find a single face to say sorry to. It was just noise, and it pressed on me like a wall. I stood by the fence, frozen. Then our coach pushed through, put his arm round me, and walked me to the bus. He sat with me all the way home and told my father what had happened that same evening. He said, "A crowd has no face, Raghav. But you do." I've never forgotten either the crowd or him.

qa.q: What did Raghav drop in the district final?
qa.a: Raghav dropped the catch that lost them the cup.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling by the fence?
qa.a: Raghav felt overwhelmed and frozen, crushed by a crowd with no single face to reason with.

qa.q: Why was the coach's response a turning point in Raghav's story?
qa.a: The coach protected Raghav at once, stayed with him and told his father that same evening, so he wasn't left alone with the crowd's hostility.

qa.q: How might Raghav's father have felt hearing from the coach that evening?
qa.a: His father likely felt worried for his son and grateful that the coach had stayed with him.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a teenager, being booed by hundreds after dropping a catch, feeling overwhelmed with no one to reason with, and an adult's same-day support.

passage: It started with one screenshot. By 9 pm last April, my phone had a hundred and forty messages from numbers I didn't know, all about a rumour that I had cheated in the science exam. I'm Jasleen, and I've never been so frightened of a buzzing sound. There was no one person to explain to; every time I replied to one, ten more came. It was like drowning in a crowd without faces. I put the phone in a drawer and sat on the bathroom floor. My cousin Gurpreet found me and didn't ask questions. She took the phone, sat with me and called my mother in from the kitchen. Mummy read ten messages, took screenshots, blocked the numbers and phoned my class teacher that same night. The next morning the principal spoke to the class. The messages stopped. I still flinch at notifications sometimes.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel as the messages kept coming?

School counsellor's note, Tuesday, 3:40 pm.
Varun brought Mahima to my office after lunch. About fifteen senior students had surrounded her near the canteen, shouting about a post they believed she had written about their teacher. Mahima said she tried to explain, but each time she spoke to one, others shouted over her. 'There was no one to talk to. Just noise.' She was shaking and hadn't eaten. I stayed with her, got her water and food, and told her plainly that this was not her fault. With her agreement I informed the vice-principal, who spoke to the senior group before dismissal, and I phoned her mother, who collected her at 4. Varun stayed with her until then. Plan: the vice-principal meets the seniors' parents tomorrow; I will see Mahima first thing in the morning.

qa.q: How many seniors surrounded Mahima?
qa.a: About fifteen senior students.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when every attempt to explain was shouted over?
qa.a: Mahima felt overwhelmed and frightened, shaking because there was no single person to reason with.

qa.q: What made the counsellor's response strong?
qa.a: Staying with Mahima, telling her it wasn't her fault, and informing the vice-principal and her mother the same afternoon.

qa.q: What did Varun do for Mahima?
qa.a: Varun brought her to the counsellor and stayed with her until her mother came, so she wasn't alone.

grounding: A counsellor's note records a student overwhelmed by a hostile crowd of seniors and the same-day protective response.

passage:
Saturday night.
Diary, today was the worst. I posted my first comic on the art site, and by lunch it had three hundred comments. Not nice ones. Someone shared it to a big meme page, and strangers were calling my drawing trash, telling me to quit, pasting my face into jokes. I kept refreshing, trying to answer, but for every one I answered, twenty more came. There's nobody to argue with in a crowd like that. I cried so hard I got hiccups. My brother Naveen saw my face at dinner and made me show him. He didn't laugh. He went straight to Papa. Papa helped me set the post to private, report the page and block everyone, and he said, 'None of these people know you. We do.' He sat with me till I fell asleep. Tomorrow we tell my art teacher too.
Hansa

qa.q: How many comments did the comic have by lunch?
qa.a: Three hundred comments.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel as the comments kept coming?
qa.a: Hansa felt overwhelmed and crushed, crying till hiccups came, with no one to reason with in the crowd.

qa.q: What did Papa's response get right?
qa.a: He acted that same evening: making the post private, reporting the page, blocking, reassuring Hansa and staying close until sleep.

qa.q: How did Naveen react when he saw Hansa's face?
qa.a: Naveen was worried and serious, didn't laugh, and went straight to Papa.

grounding: A teenager's diary records being mobbed online by strangers with no one to reason with, and the family's same-evening response.
